title: Tap one wire, freeze the rest
allegory: Path patching is testing one hallway in an office: send a doctored memo from Alice straight to Bob, order everyone else to repeat exactly what they said on the good day, and see whether Bob's decision changes.
map: the direct hallway from Alice to Bob
the edge from a sender head to a receiver, such as a name mover's queries
a doctored memo sent down that hallway only
the sender's corrupted output reaching the receiver by direct paths
everyone else repeats what they said on the good day
every other attention head frozen at its clean value
the change in the metric, e.g. the logit difference

chapters.name: Who talks to whom?
chapters.note: they both matter... but are they connected?

cap.1: You know which workers matter. But does Alice matter because she briefs Bob, or for some other reason? A list of important people is not an org chart.
cap.2: Activation patching said heads in layers 7 and 8 matter for IOI and that 9.6 and 9.9 write the answer. It could not say whether the first group acts on the second.
cap.3: Activation patching measures a node's total effect, mixing every downstream route. Establishing an edge A → B needs an intervention restricted to one path.

cap.1: So send a doctored memo down one hallway only, Alice to Bob, and order everyone else to repeat exactly what they said on the good day. Does Bob change?
cap.2: Path patching: corrupt the sender, but only along its direct route to one receiver. Every other head is frozen at its clean value, so the corruption can't sneak round another way.
cap.3: Replace the sender-to-receiver direct input with its corrupted value while all other routes stay clean. In Wang et al.'s formulation MLPs count as part of the direct path.

cap.1: Three runs: record a good day and a bad day; replay the good day with only Alice's memo swapped, others frozen; hand Bob what he heard, and measure.
cap.2: 1) Cache clean and corrupted runs. 2) Sender corrupted, other heads frozen clean, MLPs recompute; cache the receiver's input. 3) Run clean with that input injected; score it.
cap.3: Pass 2 computes the receiver's input under a sender-only corruption along direct paths; pass 3 injects it into a clean run. Sweep the sender over all 144 heads for a heatmap.

cap.1: In the name puzzle, tapping lines to the final answer lights up 9.6, 9.9 and 10.0. Tapping lines into their questions lights up a group in layers 7 and 8.
cap.2: Receiver = final residual stream: name movers 9.6, 9.9, 10.0 light up. Receiver = those heads' queries: S-inhibition heads 7.3, 7.9, 8.6, 8.10. Keys and values show much less.
cap.3: Q-composition, not K or V: S-inhibition heads change where name movers look, not what they find. Path patching also exposed duplicate-token heads K-composing into S-inhibition keys.

chapters.name: Forgot to freeze
chapters.verdict: Freezing is not an optimisation; it is the whole method.

cap.1: Let the other workers react to the doctored memo and the rumour spreads down every hallway. You are back to testing Alice as a whole.
cap.2: Skip the freezing in pass 2 and the heatmap looks like activation patching. Sanity checks: an irrelevant sender gives about 0; receiver = final residual recovers the name movers.
cap.3: Without freezing, pass 2 measures the sender's total effect, identical to node patching. Clamping non-sender, non-receiver heads is what restricts the intervention to direct paths.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: From a list of heads to a wiring diagram
Queries vs keys vs values: where vs what
Claims you can test, edge by edge

cap.1: Knowing who talks to whom turns 'these parts matter' into an explanation, and an explanation is what lets you steer a model on purpose.
cap.2: Path patching is the step from important heads to a circuit graph. Automated circuit discovery runs this same edge-by-edge sweep as a search.
cap.3: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2023) made 'behaviour is localised to these paths' a precise, testable claim. Edge-level evidence is what makes circuit hypotheses falsifiable and interventions targeted.

coda.title: Sender S reaches receiver R directly and via head H. What does each method report?

readouts.label: path patching reports
readouts.f: (a + (1 - fr)*v).toFixed(2) + (fr ? ' (direct edge only)' : ' (leaked: this is the total effect)')

caption.1: The freeze switch starts off, so path patching reports the same as whole-node patching. Flip it on: now it reports only the direct edge, however big the detour.
caption.2: Set the direct edge to 0 and the detour high: activation patching says S matters a lot, frozen path patching says S → R is nothing. S matters, just not through this wire.
caption.3: Toy linear model: total effect = direct + indirect. Freezing non-sender heads in pass 2 zeroes the indirect term, so the estimate is the direct-edge effect alone.

where_else: IOI: turning a list of important heads into a circuit graph
Automated circuit discovery: this edge-by-edge sweep run as a search
Telling Q-, K- and V-composition apart by patching queries, keys or values
Outside ML: mediation analysis, splitting a cause's direct effect from its effect through a middleman

hamming.what: Changing only what one component sends directly to another, with every other attention head frozen at its clean value, to measure an edge instead of a node.
hamming.when: Once you already suspect who talks to whom, after activation patching has told you which components matter.
hamming.why: A list of important parts is not a mechanism; edges are, and only an edge-level intervention can tell 'A matters via B' from 'A matters some other way'.

object.title: The switchboard
object.subtitle: The IOI circuit as a board of lines between groups of heads, with one line tapped and everyone else frozen.

cap.1: The name puzzle's switchboard: each line is a route one group of heads uses to reach another.
cap.2: Edges found by path patching in IOI: S-inhibition → name movers (queries) → logits.
cap.3: Receiver resid_post recovers the name movers; receiver = their queries recovers the S-inhibition heads.

cap.1: Tap this one line: swap what the S-inhibition heads send straight to the name movers, and keep everything else as it was.
cap.2: Sender = S-inhibition heads, receiver = name movers' queries, all other heads frozen at clean values.
cap.3: Patching into queries rather than keys or values isolates Q-composition: the signal changes where name movers attend.

cap.1: The grey block is everyone else, frozen to repeat the good day. Without it, the swap would leak down every other line.
cap.2: Freezing the non-sender, non-receiver heads is what makes this an edge measurement, not a node measurement.
cap.3: MLPs recompute (they sit on the direct path in Wang et al.'s formulation); attention heads are clamped to clean activations.

cap.1: Further back, duplicate-token heads feed the S-inhibition heads' keys: a line that whole-node patching had missed.
cap.2: Path patching recovered K-composition from duplicate-token heads into S-inhibition keys, which activation patching had suggested was absent.
cap.3: Duplicate-token heads write a 'duplicated' flag with no identity or position information, and the S-inhibition keys read it.

predict.q: You skip freezing the other heads. What does your path-patching heatmap look like?

options.t: Like activation patching: total effects everywhere
Cleaner: only the edge you wanted

predict.why: Unfrozen heads recompute from the corrupted sender and carry the change down every indirect route.

predict.q: Patching into the name movers' queries lights up the S-inhibition heads; keys and values show much less. What does that tell you?

options.t: They change where the name movers look
They change what the name movers copy

predict.why: Queries decide where a head attends; values decide what it moves. The signal arrives through queries: Q-composition.

predict.q: A head has a big activation-patching effect but near-zero path patching into head B. What follows?

options.t: It matters, but not through its direct line to B

predict.why: Activation patching measures the total effect over all routes; path patching measures one edge. Its influence goes some other way.

object.where: Anywhere you must test one link with the rest held steady: a single hand-off in a pipeline, one wire on a circuit board.
